description: We are SONIX, a team of 5 first-year Computer Science and Engineering students from Samrat Ashok Technological Institute (SATI), Vidisha. We are curious, fast learners who turn ideas into working projects with teamwork and modern AI tools. We are passionate about making NASA's Earth data easier to understand through visuals and sound. Our team is complete.
summary: SONIX: The Earth Information Jukebox lets people hear how Earth is changing. We turn 146 years of real NASA GISS temperature data (GISTEMP v4, 1880 to 2025) into sound with one fixed rule: a warmer year plays a higher note, from 220 Hz to 880 Hz. A rotating 3D Earth, a timeline and a live sound wave move together, so users can see and hear the same data. We also pair NASA Scientific Visualization Studio frames, such as night lights and ocean currents, with music that follows each frame's colour and brightness. SONIX is built for accessibility first: it works with a keyboard, screen readers and spoken descriptions, so blind and low-vision users can explore climate data too. Features like Birth Year, Compare and a classroom mode make the story personal and easy to teach. Every number comes from validated NASA data, and the app explains its own limits.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SONIX is a web app that lets people hear climate change. It reads NASA's global temperature record from 1880 to 2025 and plays one note per year. A warmer year gives a higher pitch. Users can press play to hear the whole time-lapse, jump to any year, compare two years, or enter their birth year and hear how Earth has changed since then. A second part, the NASA Frames tab, pairs NASA Scientific Visualization Studio frames (city lights, ocean currents) with music generated from each frame's colour and brightness.

WHY IT MATTERS (IMPACT)

Most climate data is shown as charts and maps. That leaves out blind and low-vision users, and it is easy for anyone to scroll past. Sound is personal and memorable. SONIX helps students, teachers and the general public understand long-term warming in seconds. A classroom mode, an explainer in English and Hindi [CONFIRM], and shareable links make it easy for teachers to use. Because it runs in the browser, it needs no installation.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: we download NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 (Land-Ocean Temperature Index, annual mean, baseline 1951-1980) and save it with a fetch date and source.

2. Validation: a script checks 146 consecutive years, no gaps, no duplicates and all values finite.

3. Mapping: temperature change from -0.5 C to +1.3 C maps linearly to 220 Hz to 880 Hz. For example, +0.90 C is about 733 Hz. The rule is fixed and unit-tested.

4. Sound: the Web Audio API makes every sound live in the browser. There are no audio files.

5. Frames: for NASA SVS frames, the app reads colour, brightness and edges, and turns them into mood, tempo and timbre. The temperature data stays the tonal centre. [CONFIRM: describe exactly what your Frame-to-Sound does]

6. Display: a 3D Earth built with Three.js, a timeline with warming stripes, a chart and a live sound wave all move together.

TECHNOLOGIES

Web Audio API, Three.js, TypeScript, Vite, [React - CONFIRM], Vitest for tests, HTML and CSS, [hosting: Vercel / GitHub Pages]. Data: NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 and NASA SVS visualizations. No backend and no API keys.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Climate data as a jukebox: you listen to Earth, not just look at it.

- One honest rule for sound, so the music is the data.

- A "Birth Year" feature that makes the global story personal.

- NASA frames shape the music, and the NASA data keeps the key and pitch.

- Dark and light themes, and a 100-second auto-tour [CONFIRM] for demos.

SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNICAL VALIDITY

- Every number in the interface is computed from the loaded NASA data.

- A Method and Limitations panel states the source, baseline, formula and limits.

- Limits we state clearly: global annual mean only, not local weather, not a forecast, pitch is an encoding and not a physical measurement. The glow colour on the globe is an artistic indicator.

- Tests cover the mapping formula, the data validator and the comparison logic.

RELEVANCE TO THE CHALLENGE

The challenge asks for an Earth Jukebox that pairs NASA Earth Information Center visuals with sound made in real time, with accessibility as a core theme and a clear explanation of why. SONIX does this with NASA temperature data, NASA SVS frames, live synthesized sound, keyboard and screen-reader support, and an on-screen explanation of every choice.

ACCESSIBILITY

Full keyboard use, screen-reader announcements for every year, optional spoken descriptions, reduced motion, high contrast, and a "listen without looking" mode [CONFIRM]. Colour is never the only signal; numbers are always shown.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

Planned (not yet built): more NASA datasets such as wind, rainfall, wildfires and ocean heat, each with its own sound design, and user testing with blind and low-vision listeners.

TEAM

SONIX: [ Member names and roles ], [ College / organisation ], Bhopal local event.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

We used Google Antigravity ([model - CONFIRM]) to generate and edit parts of the code, and Claude to help plan, write prompts, draft text and build our presentation. [The SONIX logo was created with <tool> and is marked AI-generated - CONFIRM.] All sounds are synthesized by our own code in the browser; no AI audio model was used. The team reviewed, tested and verified all data, numbers and credits.
